simple: where something is and which way it faces, in space.
analogy: where your head is and where your face points.
precise: the position and orientation of a frame B relative to a frame A, written as the rigid transform TAB = [RAB tAB; 0 1] with a 3 × 3 rotation and a 3-vector; six independent numbers in all.
source: D1 of F9-23 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F9-23 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: a turn plus a shift that never stretches or mirrors anything.
analogy: moving your whole hand without bending it.
precise: a map p ↦ Rp + t with R a rotation (RTR = I, det R = +1); the set of these maps with composition is the special Euclidean group SE(3). Products and inverses stay in the set.
source: B1 of F9-23 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); D1 of F9-23 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs)

simple: a family tree of all the frames on a robot, each one attached to exactly one parent.
analogy: eyes on head, head on neck, neck on body, body in the room.
precise: a rooted tree whose nodes are frames and whose edges store Tparent,child; the transform between any two frames is the product along the unique path between them, with edges walked towards the root inverted. MA201 introduced it (F0-54); here it becomes code.
source: D1 of F9-23 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); S1 of F9-23 (ROS 2 documentation — not opened in this build, pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: a link that never changes (a bolted bracket) versus one that changes all the time (the robot's place in the room, a joint).
analogy: your eye in your head never moves relative to the skull; your head on your neck turns.
precise: a static edge is valid for all time; a dynamic edge is a time series of stamped transforms, and a lookup must say for which time it wants the answer.
source: S1 of F9-23 (ROS 2 documentation — not opened in this build, pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); R2 of F9-23 (lab run in this build, simulated robot, untested on hardware)

simple: measuring exactly where a sensor is bolted on and which way it points.
analogy: knowing exactly where your eyes are on your face.
precise: estimating the static transform between a sensor's frame and the robot's base frame, from measurements, as opposed to the sensor's internal (intrinsic) parameters.
source: B1 of F9-23 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); D1 of F9-23 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs)

simple: the ROS 2 library that keeps the robot's frame tree and answers "where is this frame relative to that one, at this time?".
analogy: the part of your brain that always knows where your head is on your body.
precise: the transform library of ROS 2; its exact API and conventions are not verified in this build (unverified box in Layer 3).
source: S1 of F9-23 (ROS 2 documentation — not opened in this build, pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: how far apart the two driven wheels are.
analogy: the distance between the two big wheels of a wheelchair.
precise: the distance W between the contact points of the left and right driven wheels, measured along the axle; it sets how fast a speed difference turns the robot. Some texts use the half-width instead; check which one a formula uses.
source: D1 of F9-24 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F9-24 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: how fast the robot goes forward and how fast it turns.
analogy: "roll forward briskly while curving left gently".
precise: the pair (v, ω): forward speed of the axle midpoint along the body x axis (m/s) and turn rate about the vertical axis (rad/s); a planar special case of the twist of "Modern Robotics".
source: B1 of F9-24 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); D1 of F9-24 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs)

simple: from wheel speeds to robot motion.
analogy: feeling how hard each hand pushed and knowing how the chair moved.
precise: v = r(ωR + ωL)/2, ω = r(ωR − ωL)/W for wheel radius r and wheel angular speeds ωL, ωR.
source: D1 of F9-24 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F9-24 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: from wanted robot motion to wheel speeds.
analogy: deciding how hard each hand must push.
precise: ωR = (v + ωW/2)/r, ωL = (v − ωW/2)/r.
source: D1 of F9-24 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs)

simple: the point the robot is circling around at this moment.
analogy: the spot on the floor the wheelchair curves around.
precise: for ω ≠ 0, the point on the axle line at signed distance R = v/ω from the axle midpoint; R = ∞ means straight, R = 0 means spinning on the spot.
source: B1 of F9-24 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); D1 of F9-24 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs)

simple: a rule about how you may move, not about where you may be.
analogy: the wheelchair can reach any spot in the room, but never by sliding sideways.
precise: a constraint on velocities that cannot be integrated into a constraint on positions; here ẋ sin θ − ẏ cos θ = 0 (no velocity along the axle).
source: B1 of F9-24 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: working out where you are by adding up how the wheels turned.
analogy: counting your pushes in the dark.
precise: integrating the body twist computed from wheel encoders into a pose estimate TWB(t); its error grows without bound because nothing corrects it (RB201 F9-09; RB302).
source: B2 of F9-24 (Sebastian Thrun, Wolfram Burgard, Dieter Fox, "Probabilistic Robotics" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); U1 of F9-24 (University Authoring Guide course cards and internal chapters)

simple: the stiff pieces of an arm, and the hinges or slides between them.
analogy: upper arm and forearm; shoulder and elbow.
precise: a link is a rigid body; a joint constrains the relative motion of two links to one (or more) degrees of freedom. A serial arm alternates them from the base to the tool.
source: B1 of F9-25 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: a hinge that turns, and a slide that moves in a straight line.
analogy: your elbow; a drawer.
precise: a revolute joint allows rotation about a fixed axis (variable: an angle); a prismatic joint allows translation along a fixed axis (variable: a distance).
source: B1 of F9-25 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: describing the arm by its joint angles, or by where its tool is.
analogy: "shoulder up a bit, elbow bent" versus "hand on the table".
precise: joint space is the set of joint-variable vectors q; task space is the set of tool poses T(q) ∈ SE(3) (or tool positions only). Forward kinematics maps the first to the second.
source: B1 of F9-25 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); D1 of F9-25 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs)

simple: from joint angles to where the tool is.
analogy: touching your nose with your eyes closed.
precise: the map q ↦ Tbase,tool(q), here the product of each joint's fixed offset and its motion along the chain.
source: B1 of F9-25 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); D1 of F9-25 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs)

simple: the arm's pose when every joint reads zero.
analogy: standing with your arm stretched out sideways, the position you call "zero".
precise: the configuration q = 0 and its tool pose M = T(0); which physical pose is "zero" is a choice made by the designer and fixed by the encoders' zero (homing).
source: B1 of F9-25 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: a line in space plus a rule for how a joint moves along or around it.
analogy: the line through your elbow's hinge.
precise: S = (ω, v) ∈ ℝ6; for a revolute joint, ω is the unit axis direction and v = −ω × p for any point p on the axis, all expressed in the base frame at the home configuration.
source: B1 of F9-25 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); R2 of F9-25 (lab run in this build, simulated robot, untested on hardware)

simple: a formula that gets the tool pose by turning each joint about its own line, starting from the home pose.
analogy: starting from "arm out sideways", turn the shoulder, then the elbow, and see where the hand ends up.
precise: T(q) = e[S1]q1 e[S2]q2 ⋯ e[Sn]qn M, where each factor is the rigid motion "rotate by qi about screw axis Si".
source: B1 of F9-25 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); R2 of F9-25 (lab run in this build, simulated robot, untested on hardware)

simple: an older, compact recipe that describes each link with four numbers.
analogy: a standard form for writing down an arm.
precise: a convention that attaches a frame to each link by fixed rules so that each link transform is a product of two rotations and two translations with four parameters; several variants exist (often called classic and modified), and they are not interchangeable.
source: B1 of F9-25 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: from where the tool must be to the joint angles that put it there.
analogy: deciding how to bend shoulder and elbow to touch the teapot.
precise: finding q with T(q) = Ttarget (or with the tool position equal to a target point); there may be zero, finitely many, or infinitely many solutions.
source: B1 of F9-26 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: all the places the tool can reach.
analogy: everything you can touch without stepping.
precise: the set of tool positions (or poses) T(q) over all allowed q; for a planar 2R arm without joint limits, the annulus |L1 − L2| ≤ d ≤ L1 + L2 around the shoulder.
source: B1 of F9-26 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); D1 of F9-26 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs)

simple: one of the different postures that reach the same target.
analogy: Sami's elbow down, Lea's elbow up.
precise: one of the discrete solution families of an IK problem; for the planar 2R arm, the sign of sin θ2. Which one is called "up" depends on the arm and the target; this chapter defines it in Layer 2.
source: D1 of F9-26 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs)

simple: an angle finder that knows which quarter of the circle you are in.
analogy: a compass that tells north-east from south-west.
precise: atan2(y, x) returns the angle of the vector (x, y) in (−π, π], using the signs of both arguments; atan(y/x) loses the quadrant and fails at x = 0.
source: S1 of F9-26 (ISO/IEC 14882 — not opened in this build, pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); D1 of F9-26 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs)

simple: guess the angles, see how far off the tool is, correct the guess, repeat.
analogy: reaching in the dark: move, feel how far you are from the handle, adjust.
precise: iterate q ← q + Δq with J(q)Δq ≈ e (e = target − FK(q)); damped least squares solves (JTJ + λ2I)Δq = JTe, which stays well-behaved when J is nearly singular.
source: B1 of F9-26 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); R2 of F9-26 (lab run in this build, simulated robot, untested on hardware)

simple: an arm with more joints than the task needs.
analogy: your arm can keep your hand on the teapot while your elbow swings up and down.
precise: an arm whose number of joints exceeds the dimension of the task (for example three planar joints for a 2D position); its IK solutions form a continuous family.
source: B1 of F9-26 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: a table that says how fast the tool moves for each joint's speed.
analogy: how far your hand moves for a small twitch of the shoulder, and for a small twitch of the elbow.
precise: the matrix J(q) of partial derivatives of the forward-kinematics map, Jij = ∂xi/∂qj, so that ẋ = J(q)q̇; for full 3D poses, a 6 × n matrix mapping joint velocities to the tool's twist.
source: B1 of F9-27 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); D1 of F9-27 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs)

simple: a pose where the arm cannot move its tool in some direction, however its joints move.
analogy: Mei's fully stretched arm cannot move the cloth farther out.
precise: a configuration where J loses rank (det J = 0 for a square J); there, some tool velocities need infinite joint velocities and some tool forces need no joint torque.
source: B1 of F9-27 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: a score for how freely the tool can move in all directions at this pose.
analogy: wiping near your body (easy) versus at full stretch (hard).
precise: w = √det(JJT), equal to |det J| for a square J; zero exactly at singularities. The velocity ellipsoid {Jq̇ : |q̇| = 1} shows the direction-by-direction picture.
source: B1 of F9-27 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); D1 of F9-27 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs)

simple: the joint torques that hold a push at the tool still.
analogy: how hard your shoulder and elbow work to hold a door.
precise: for a static arm with tool force F, the joint torques that balance it are τ = JTF (up to the sign convention for "applied" versus "resisted" force), from equal power τTq̇ = FTẋ.
source: B1 of F9-27 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); D1 of F9-27 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs)

simple: moving the tool at a chosen speed by recomputing the joint speeds many times a second.
analogy: guiding your hand along a ruler while your joints sort themselves out.
precise: at every control period, set q̇ = J(q)−1(ẋdesired + K(xdesired − x)), and integrate q̇; the feedback term corrects drift.
source: B1 of F9-27 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); R3 of F9-27 (lab run in this build, simulated robot, untested on hardware)

simple: a softened inverse that never asks for crazy joint speeds.
analogy: near full stretch, Mei accepts that the cloth lags a little instead of whipping her arm.
precise: q̇ = JT(JJT + λ2I)−1ẋ; equal to J−1ẋ when λ = 0 and J is invertible, bounded for every J when λ > 0, at the cost of a tracking error near singularities.
source: B1 of F9-27 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); R2 of F9-27 (lab run in this build, simulated robot, untested on hardware)

simple: the rule that links joint torques to how the arm speeds up.
analogy: how hard your shoulder must work to start, stop and hold a swinging bag.
precise: M(q)q̈ + c(q, q̇) + g(q) = τ for an open chain without friction, where τ is the vector of joint torques.
source: B1 of F9-28 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); D1 of F9-28 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs)

simple: how hard each joint is to speed up, and how speeding up one joint pushes on the others.
analogy: a bag held far out is harder to swing than one held close.
precise: the symmetric, positive-definite matrix M(q) with kinetic energy ½q̇TM(q)q̇; it depends on the configuration.
source: B1 of F9-28 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); D1 of F9-28 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs)

simple: pushes between joints that appear only while the arm moves.
analogy: the swinging bag tugging your elbow open.
precise: the vector c(q, q̇), quadratic in the joint velocities: terms in q̇i2 are centrifugal, terms in q̇iq̇j (i ≠ j) are Coriolis.
source: B1 of F9-28 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: the torque each joint needs to hold the arm still against its own weight.
analogy: the burning shoulder holding the bag at arm's length.
precise: g(q) = ∂P/∂q, the gradient of the potential energy P(q) with respect to the joint angles.
source: B1 of F9-28 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); D1 of F9-28 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs)

simple: inverse: "what torques give this motion?"; forward: "what motion do these torques give?".
analogy: planning how hard to pull, versus feeling where the bag goes when you pull.
precise: inverse dynamics evaluates τ = M q̈ + c + g; forward dynamics solves M q̈ = τ − c − g for q̈ and is integrated in time to simulate.
source: B1 of F9-28 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: a test that a simulated arm with no motors and no friction keeps its total energy.
analogy: a playground swing never goes higher than where it was let go.
precise: with τ = 0 and no dissipation, E = ½q̇TMq̇ + P(q) is constant along exact solutions; the change of E in a simulation measures integration error.
source: D1 of F9-28 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); R1 of F9-28 (lab run in this build, simulated robot, untested on hardware)

simple: a text file that lists a robot's parts, how they are joined, and how much they weigh.
analogy: the bicycle's parts list with attachment instructions.
precise: a machine-readable description of a robot's kinematic tree (links and joints with their fixed offsets, axes and limits) and, optionally, inertial, visual and collision data; read by visualisers, simulators, planners and frame publishers.
source: D1 of F9-29 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); S1 of F9-29 (The URDF specification and the ROS 2 documentation for robot descriptions — not opened in this build, pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: the XML format ROS uses for one robot's parts list.
analogy: a parts list that only allows a tree: every part hangs off exactly one other part.
precise: an XML format with a robot element containing link and joint elements; the joints must form a tree with one root link. Element names in this chapter are unverified (see the box in Layer 3).
source: S1 of F9-29 (The URDF specification and the ROS 2 documentation for robot descriptions — not opened in this build, pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: a richer XML format that can describe whole worlds for a simulator.
analogy: the plan for the whole bike shed, not only one bicycle.
precise: an XML format for worlds containing several models, lights and physics settings; models may include closed kinematic chains and sensors. Described conceptually only in this chapter (unverified).
source: S2 of F9-29 (The SDF specification — not opened in this build, pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: where the child part sits on the parent part when the joint is at zero.
analogy: "the fork is attached 5 cm in front of the frame's top, tilted back".
precise: the fixed transform Tparent,joint from the joint frame to the parent link frame, given as a translation xyz and a rotation rpy; the joint's motion is applied after it, about the joint's axis in the joint frame.
source: D1 of F9-29 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); S1 of F9-29 (The URDF specification and the ROS 2 documentation for robot descriptions — not opened in this build, pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: three angles that say how a part is turned: about x, about y and about z.
analogy: tipping a bicycle sideways (roll), nose up or down (pitch), and turning it left or right (yaw).
precise: in this chapter's reader, rotation R = Rz(yaw)Ry(pitch)Rx(roll) with angles in radians; that this matches URDF is an assumption (unverified box).
source: D1 of F9-29 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); S1 of F9-29 (The URDF specification and the ROS 2 documentation for robot descriptions — not opened in this build, pending verification (dossier gate G1 open))

simple: how a joint may move: turn with limits, turn for ever, slide, or not at all.
analogy: the fork (limited turn), a wheel (endless turn), a seat post (slide when loosened), the handlebar clamp (fixed).
precise: revolute: rotation about the axis within [lower, upper]; continuous: unlimited rotation; prismatic: translation along the axis; fixed: no motion, the origin alone.
source: S1 of F9-29 (The URDF specification and the ROS 2 documentation for robot descriptions — not opened in this build, pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)); D1 of F9-29 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs)
